input
rows.explainer: GiveWell guesstimate. There will be a lot of variation in how efficacious treaments are for the range of potential non-malaria conditions but this is meant to be a central estimate. We think most non-malarial patients who get some treatment will get empirical treatment that's partially effective rather than targeted treatment that's highly effective. There are real benefits for the minority who need antibiotics and accidentally get appropriate ones, but the benefits are diluted across the majority who either don't need antibiotics or get inappropriate ones. Hopkins et al. 2017 shows that a lot of the antibiotic dispensing that happens is poorly targeted: "In the studies we analysed, choice of antibacterial was inevitably untargeted as health workers in these settings do not have access to facilities to confirm diagnoses and identify pathogens nor to epidemiological data to help guide ant

rows.label: calc
rows.explainer: GiveWell guesstimate. We are highly unsure what the precise CFR is for the relevant non-malaria febrile illnesses that patients may present with. We believe that the non-malaria illnesses likely have a lower CFR than malaria, but this is speculative. We also think that the under-5 and over-5 CFRs would be different but haven't attempted to estimate the differences here.

rows.label: input
rows.explainer: GiveWell guesstimate informed by Bruxvoort et al. 2017 figure 2 left-hand panel (without mRDT interventions column). The rates of presumptive ACT treatment range from 20-100%. We guess that 70-90% of febrile cases are given presumptive malaria treatment in government facilities and that the highest rates of presumptive treatment occur in rural settings with limited healthcare access and higher perceived malaria risk. We also assume that the rate of presumptive ACT use is not correlated with truly having malaria (ie. we assume a uniform rate of ACT for all suspected malaria cases).

rows.label: input
rows.explainer: GiveWell guesstimate. We think that malaria control interventions have a larger impact on all-cause mortality than on malaria-specific mortality. For example, malaria can increase the risk of mortality associated with malnutrition or other infectious diseases. We're very uncertain what the exact magnitude of this adjustment should be. For our ITN CEA we use 0.75 as our baseline (more on that here). For malaria treatment, like ACTs, we think this value should be less than 0.75 because 1) prevention stops infections before they can weaken health status, while treatment acts after someone is already compromised and 2) in more recent analyses, we've found that indirect death adjustments for ITNs/SMC tend to be lower than 0.75 when factoring in the share of deaths due to malaria.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly
rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years.
